title: Pandas: clean, transform, group, merge
summary: Use pandas DataFrames to load messy data, clean it, transform columns, group and aggregate, then merge tables together.
objectives: Load data into a DataFrame and inspect it with head, info and describe
Select rows and columns using loc and iloc
Clean missing values with dropna and fillna
Transform columns with vectorised operations and assign
Summarise data with groupby and aggregation
Combine tables with merge on a shared key
Save a cleaned DataFrame back to CSV

quiz.q: What is the primary 2D data structure in pandas?
quiz.why: A DataFrame is the table-like 2D structure with rows and labelled columns; a Series is a single column.

quiz.q: Which method selects rows and columns by their labels?
quiz.why: loc selects by label; iloc selects by integer position. df.loc[2, 'age'] uses labels.

quiz.answer: A Series of total sales for each city, indexed by city.
quiz.why: groupby splits rows by city, then sum aggregates the sales column within each group into one value per city.

quiz.q: Which call fills missing values with 0 instead of deleting rows?
quiz.why: fillna(0) replaces NaN with 0 and keeps every row; dropna would remove rows containing missing values.

quiz.q: In df.merge(other, on='id', how='left'), what does how='left' do?
quiz.answer: It keeps every row from the left DataFrame and attaches matching rows from the right, filling NaN where there is no match.
quiz.why: A left join preserves all left-side rows; unmatched right-side columns become NaN, like a SQL LEFT JOIN.

quiz.q: Why are pandas vectorised operations like df['a'] * 2 preferred over a Python for-loop?
quiz.answer: They run in fast compiled C code over the whole column at once, so they are much faster and shorter than looping row by row.
quiz.why: Vectorisation avoids slow per-row Python overhead and is the idiomatic, performant way to transform columns.

body_markdown:
## What is pandas?

**pandas** is the standard Python library for working with tabular data — the kind you find in spreadsheets, CSV files and SQL tables. Its core object is the **DataFrame**: rows and labelled columns, like a sheet in Excel but programmable.

As a maths graduate, think of a DataFrame as a matrix where every column has a name and can hold a different type. Most real data science work is *getting the data into shape* before any modelling happens.

```python
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("sales.csv")
print(df.head())     # first 5 rows
print(df.info())     # columns, types, missing counts
print(df.describe()) # summary stats for numeric columns
```

## Selecting data

Use `loc` to select by **label** and `iloc` to select by **integer position**. You can filter rows with a boolean condition, which is how you ask questions of your data.

```python
df["price"]              # one column (a Series)
df.loc[0, "price"]       # row label 0, column 'price'
df.iloc[0, 2]            # first row, third column
df[df["price"] > 100]    # rows where price exceeds 100
```

## Cleaning missing data

Real data is messy. Missing values show up as **NaN**. You either drop them or fill them — the right choice depends on the column.

```python
df.isna().sum()             # count missing per column
df = df.dropna(subset=["price"])   # drop rows missing price
df["city"] = df["city"].fillna("unknown")
```

## Transforming columns

Do maths on whole columns at once — this is **vectorisation**, and it is far faster and clearer than a Python loop. Use `assign` or direct assignment to add new columns.

```python
df["total"] = df["price"] * df["quantity"]
df["price_gbp"] = df["price"].round(2)
df["name"] = df["name"].str.strip().str.title()
```

## Grouping and aggregating

`groupby` follows a **split–apply–combine** pattern: split rows into groups, apply a function to each group, combine the results. This is how you turn raw rows into insight.

```python
df.groupby("city")["total"].sum()
df.groupby("city").agg(
    revenue=("total", "sum"),
    orders=("total", "count"),
)
```

## Merging tables

Data often lives across several tables. `merge` joins them on a shared **key**, exactly like a SQL join. `how` controls which rows are kept: inner, left, right or outer.

```python
orders = pd.read_csv("orders.csv")
customers = pd.read_csv("customers.csv")
joined = orders.merge(customers, on="customer_id", how="left")
joined.to_csv("orders_clean.csv", index=False)
```

## Your task

Take a CSV with missing values, **clean it, add one new column, group by a category, and merge in a second table**.

slides.narration: Welcome back. In this lesson we meet pandas, the workhorse library for handling tabular data in Python. This is the day-to-day work of nearly every data and A I job, so it's worth getting comfortable here.

slides.title: Inspect your data first
bullets: head shows the first few rows.
info lists columns, types and missing counts.
describe gives summary statistics.
Always look before you transform.
slides.code:
df.head()       # first 5 rows
df.info()       # types and nulls
df.describe()   # numeric summary
slides.narration: Before changing anything, always look at your data. Head shows the first five rows so you can eyeball the shape. Info lists every column, its type, and how many values are missing. Describe gives you quick statistics like mean, min and max for the numeric columns. Looking first saves you from cleaning the wrong thing.

slides.title: Selecting rows and columns
bullets: loc selects by label.
iloc selects by integer position.
Filter rows with a boolean condition.
A single column is called a Series.
slides.narration: To pull out parts of the table, use loc to select by label and iloc to select by integer position. So loc zero comma price gives the price in row labelled zero, while iloc zero comma two gives the first row and third column by position. The most useful trick is filtering with a condition: df where price is greater than one hundred returns just the rows that match.

slides.title: Cleaning missing data
bullets: Missing values appear as NaN.
isna().sum() counts them per column.
dropna removes rows; fillna replaces them.
Choose per column, not blindly.
slides.narration: Real data is messy, and missing values show up as NaN. Start by counting them with is N A dot sum, which tells you how bad it is per column. Then you choose: dropna removes rows with missing values, while fillna replaces them with something sensible. Here we drop rows missing a price, but fill a missing city with the word unknown. The right choice depends on the column.

slides.title: Transforming columns
bullets: Do maths on whole columns at once.
This is vectorisation: fast and clear.
Assign creates new columns.
String methods live under .str.
slides.narration: Now we transform. The pandas way is to operate on a whole column at once. Multiplying price by quantity creates a total column for every row in one line. This is called vectorisation, and it runs in fast compiled code, far quicker and clearer than a Python loop. For text, the dot s t r accessor gives you string tools like strip and title to tidy up names.

slides.title: Grouping and aggregating
bullets: groupby splits rows into groups.
Then apply a function like sum or mean.
Combine results into one row per group.
This is split, apply, combine.
slides.narration: Grouping is how you turn raw rows into insight. Groupby follows a pattern called split, apply, combine: split the rows into groups, apply a function to each group, then combine the results. So groupby city, then total, then sum gives you total sales per city in one tidy result. The agg method lets you compute several named summaries at once.

slides.title: Merging tables
bullets: merge joins two tables on a shared key.
Just like a SQL join.
how controls which rows are kept.
left keeps all rows from the left table.
slides.narration: Data usually lives across several tables, so we join them with merge. You give it the key column they share, like customer underscore i d, and pandas lines up the matching rows. This is exactly like a join in S Q L. The how argument decides which rows survive: a left join keeps every row from the left table and attaches matching data from the right, leaving NaN where there's no match.

slides.title: Saving your work
bullets: Write a cleaned DataFrame back to CSV.
Use index=False to skip the row numbers.
Now it is ready for analysis or a model.
Reproducible: re-run the whole script.
slides.narration: Once your data is clean and merged, save it. To underscore C S V writes the DataFrame to a file, and passing index equals False stops pandas from adding an extra column of row numbers. The beauty of doing this in a script is that it's reproducible: anyone can re-run it and get the same clean output, which is the heart of good data work.

slides.title: Common mistakes
bullets: Confusing loc (labels) with iloc (positions).
Looping over rows instead of vectorising.
Dropping rows when filling would be better.
Forgetting index=False when saving.
slides.narration: Let's flag the traps. One: mixing up loc and iloc. Loc uses labels, iloc uses positions. Two: writing a slow Python loop when a single vectorised operation would do. Three: blindly dropping rows when filling the gap is smarter. And four: forgetting index equals False, which leaves a junk column in your saved file. Watch these and your pandas code will stay clean and fast.
